offence_severity: life imprisonment together with a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/-, and in default, simple imprisonment of one year; life imprisonment together with a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/-, and in default, simple imprisonment of one year; three years’ rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of Rs. 25,000/-, and in default, simple imprisonment of six months; one year’s rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of Rs. 5,000/-, and in default simple imprisonment of three months; three years’ rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of Rs. 5,000/- and in default, simple imprisonment of one month; one year’s rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of Rs. 5,000/- and in default, simple imprisonment of one month; six months’ rigorous imprisonment together with a fine of Rs. 500/- and in default, simple imprisonment of one month
physical_harm: Injuries and death caused to witnesses, including severe injury and death of a witness during treatment
number_of_offences: Seven offences were registered against the respondent, and the number of offences finally upheld is not stated
premeditation_planning: The court found that the respondent and his followers attempted to threaten and suborn the investigating team and the witnesses, indicating premeditation and planning
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the evidence that the respondent had engaged in illegal activities inside the jail, including keeping a mobile phone and making contacts outside the jail; had engaged in criminal misconduct to hinder judicial proceedings by threatening, assaulting and murdering witnesses; and that his release on furlough may lead to a violation of public peace and tranquility.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that attempts were made to threaten and suborn the investigating team and the witnesses, and that the conduct after the trial, in jail, was not shown to be above reproach.
post_offence_conduct: The respondent was released on temporary bail for a period of three weeks on 16 April 2015 and for a period of two days on 15 February 2019. He was granted furlough in December 2020 and surrendered to the authorities after interim bail from 31 January 2021 till 3 February 2021.
bail_history: Interim bail granted from 31 January 2021 till 3 February 2021
trial_duration: Offence: 6 October 2013; Trial judgment: 30 April 2019; High Court: 2 December 2020; Supreme Court: 24 June 2021
legal_representation: Sanjiv Punalekar, Suvidutt M. S., Ankush Mahajan, Dharma Raj, Mrs. Anu B., Ms. Vijayalakshmi Raju, Mrs. Dhanya C. for the Respondent; Tushar Mehta, Kanu Agrawal, Aniruddha P. Mayee for the Appellants
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction and sentence; High Court: Released on furlough; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, order set aside
prosecution_argument: The State argued that the respondent's release on furlough would threaten public peace and tranquility due to his criminal history, including threats, assaults, and murders of witnesses, as well as his followers' potential to disrupt public order.
defence_argument: The defence contended that the High Court's previous order granting furlough was valid and that the respondent had not engaged in any illegal activities since then, and that the DGP's reasons for denying furlough were not justified.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that furlough is a discretionary remedy governed by the Bombay Furlough and Parole Rules, and that the grant of furlough must be balanced against public interest and can be refused to certain categories of prisoners.
precedent_relied_upon: State of Maharashtra v. Suresh Pandurang Darvakar (2006) 4 SCC 776; Asfaq v. State of Rajasthan (2017) 15 SCC 55; State of Haryana v. Mohinder Singh (2000) 3 SCC 394
